posts.note: Satirical open letter to UnitedHealth Group after a job rejection. Most future talk is a pun on UHG's trademarked slogan; two semi-serious litigation/MLR claims and several footnote items logged. Sarcastic footnotes 28, 29 and 31 imply UHG faces discrimination and retaliation liability; folded into notes rather than logged as separate statements.
Substack template announcement of a subscriber chat; one own-newsletter plan and one Substack product-roadmap line (Android chat 'soon').
Explainer on IRS 501(r) hospital financial assistance; present-tense description and advice only.

ERISA/ACA network-adequacy explainer; one dated claim that federal oversight returns in 2023. The rhetorical question about doctors fleeing states over malpractice insurance was not logged (question).
OCD and suicide-risk epidemiology; statistics ('14% ... will attempt suicide') are rate statements, not forecasts.
Founder advice column with a fictional 'bullshit as a service' company; generic truisms ('people are going to steal your ideas', 'at some point you'll have to pivot') not logged.
Personal memoir of childhood suicidality and bipolar diagnosis; a book-in-progress mention, one personal 'never' statement, and a 'To be continued' content promise.
Past-tense narrative of an ER visit; expectations inside the narrative are past. Only a 'To be continued' content promise.

statements.quote: not only is it less likely that I will be doing my life‘s best work, but it is, in fact, guaranteed
statements.context: UnitedHealth Group rejected the author's application for a Behavioral Medical Director role. The author jokes that because UHG trademarked the slogan 'your life's best work', it is now guaranteed he will not do his life's best work anywhere.
statements.note: Satirical pun on UHG's trademarked slogan; does not read as a real expectation. Repeated in footnote 25 ('poetic translations will not be my life's best work').

statements.quote: I will have to find a way to explain all that to my children as they become old enough to search the internet for their parents and find an entire, somewhat absurd, blog
statements.context: In a sincere passage listing career highs and lows (lawsuit, stalker, investors withdrawing), the author expects his children will one day find a blog dedicated to attacking him online and that he will need to explain it.
statements.note: Personal forward-looking statement; low forecast value.

statements.quote: This way, many many more treatments will not meet criteria for approval, without the manual labor of having to do peer-to-peer reviews
statements.context: 'Abandoning My Life's Best Work Gem #1': the author's mock proposal that UHG/Optum Insights build natural language processing software that checks prior records to stop clinicians from supplying diagnoses that fit prior-authorization rules. He claims the result would be many more denials without peer-to-peer reviews.
statements.note: Satirical proposal; conditional on a fictional software program. The causal mechanism (more denials) reads as a real belief about UHG incentives.

statements.quote: if we keep tinkering with numbers, everyone will start gaming things out in ever more economically productive ways… for UnitedHealth Group of course!
statements.context: 'Gem #2', the mock 'Approve a Claim, Deny a Claim' program in which every in-network physician also acts as a conscripted claims reviewer. The author says such incentives would make everyone game the system to UHG's benefit, then adds that the current unpaid appeals burden is 'not actually more crazy'.
statements.note: Satirical conditional inside a mock program proposal.

statements.quote: All of the above could be litigated, and even lose billions.
statements.context: 'Gem #3' lists UHG's incentives: a hiring system that collects voluntary disability disclosures and then rejects applicants (class-action disability discrimination exposure), possible retaliation in hiring, and ugly corporate email headers. The author says all of it could be litigated and UHG could lose billions.
statements.note: Semi-serious ('seriously, see the footnotes'). Footnote 31 sarcastically implies UHG 'generated a class that could take legal action'; folded here.

statements.quote: those expenses, all of those expenses , would find their way to the UnitedHealth Group balance sheet in a way that increased the total cost of doing business for their health insurance business, and thus increased the amount of profits they were allowed to make using a fixed medical loss ratio calculation
statements.context: Follows the litigation claim. The author argues that litigation losses would raise UHG's costs and, under a fixed medical loss ratio, raise the absolute profit UHG is allowed to make ('UnitedHealthCare = More Profits From More Expenses').
statements.note: Conditional on litigation losses. Restated in the closing: UHG hungers 'to be sued ... lose, and just make more money in the process' and in footnote 35.

statements.quote: That young man is now a friend, and he’s also going to train in child and adolescent psychiatry.
statements.context: Footnote 16, about a medical student with a psychiatric diagnosis whom the author inspired by disclosing his own bipolar disorder on Clubhouse. The author states the student will train in child and adolescent psychiatry.
statements.note: Third person's career plan (unnamed medical student); low forecast value.

statements.quote: turn that approach into a patentable technology which is now being brought to market by Magnus Medical
statements.context: Footnote 18, on the author's paper about rapid remission of suicidal depression with brain stimulation. He says Nolan Williams's Stanford lab completed the randomized controlled trial work on this protocol (SNT/SAINT) and turned it into a patentable technology that Magnus Medical is bringing to market.
statements.note: Borderline: present-progressive description that implies future commercialization of SNT by Magnus Medical.

statements.quote: I’ll post short prompts, thoughts, and updates that come my way, and you can jump into the discussion.
statements.context: Announcement of The Frontier Psychiatrists subscriber chat in the Substack app. The author states what he will post in the chat.
statements.note: Own-newsletter plan, largely Substack template text; coder may mark CONTROL.

statements.quote: Chat is only on iOS for now, but chat is coming to the Android app soon.
statements.context: Same announcement; 'How to get started' step 1 says the Substack chat feature is iOS-only for now and will come to the Android app soon.
statements.note: Substack boilerplate published in the author's voice; product-roadmap claim about a third-party company.

statements.quote: Federal oversight of adequacy returns in 2023.
statements.context: Explainer on ERISA-compliant health insurance. After stating that ACA rules require adequate provider networks (time/distance standards, provider ratios, wait times), the author says federal oversight of network adequacy returns in 2023.
statements.note: Bare dated assertion about federal network-adequacy oversight (likely CMS marketplace reviews).

statements.quote: It’s a big one, and the reason I’m writing a book.
statements.context: Opening of a memoir essay. The author says the social pressure on clinicians not to treat suicidal patients with evidence-based tools is the problem behind a book he is writing.
statements.note: Own project (book in progress); coder may mark CONTROL.

statements.quote: I’m never going to know what happened at the end of my sister’s life.
statements.context: The author describes his sister Alison Muir's death by opiate overdose, which was unclear as intentional or accidental, and says he will never know what happened.
Closing line of the memoir essay about childhood suicidality and the NYSPI/Columbia bipolar study; the author promises a continuation post.
statements.note: Trivial content promise; coder may mark CONTROL.
